## 1. The Hook: The Mystery of the Dancing Snake

Have you ever seen someone playing a flute-like instrument while a snake sways side to side as if it is dancing? It looks like the snake is listening to the music, right?

## 2. Socratic Thinking

Here is a puzzle for you: Snakes do not have external ears! So, if they cannot hear sounds in the air like we do, how are they 'dancing' to the music of the *been*?

content.title: How a Snake 'Hears'
content.description: A snake feels the vibrations on the ground and follows the movement of the 'been'.

text:
## 4. The Reveal: Kalbeliyas and the 'Been'

The people who have this special skill are known as the **Kalbeliyas** (the snake charmers). They don't just play the instrument called a **been**, but they also have deep knowledge of snakes. And the secret? The snake isn't actually listening to music; it reacts to the vibrations and follows the movement of the instrument!

content.definition: A community in Rajasthan that is famous for their traditional occupation of catching snakes and trading snake venom, and for their snake-like dance.
A musical instrument made from a dried gourd (lauki), traditionally played by snake charmers.

content.question: Why does a snake appear to 'dance' to the snake charmer's music?
options: It loves the sound of the flute.
It follows the movement of the instrument and feels vibrations.
It is trained to dance for food.

text:
## 6. Reflection

For generations, the Kalbeliyas have lived with snakes. They treat snakes as a part of their family, passing their knowledge from father to son. Imagine if your family had a special skill for hundreds of years. How would you feel if you suddenly had to stop doing it?

## 7. Connection: Laws and Livelihoods

The government has made a law that no one can catch or keep wild animals, including snakes. This law is very important to stop animal cruelty. However, it also means the Kalbeliyas can no longer earn their living as snake charmers. They have to find new ways to use their amazing knowledge of animals and medicinal plants to survive.

content.text:
## 8. Mastery: New Beginnings

Think of a creative way the Kalbeliyas could use their knowledge of snakes and jungle medicines to earn a living today without keeping snakes in captivity (for example, becoming forest guides or running educational shows). Write down 3 ideas!

## 1. The Hook: The Fear of Fangs

Whenever someone shouts 'Snake!', people immediately run away in fear. We often think that every single snake is deadly and will bite us. But is that really true?

## 2. Socratic Thinking

If a snake wants to bite and inject poison into its prey, how does the poison travel from its mouth deep into the other animal's body? Think about what a doctor uses to give you medicine!

content.title: Snake Fangs as Hollow Needles
content.description: Notice how the snake's fangs are hollow inside, just like a doctor's syringe.

text:
## 4. The Reveal: Fangs and the Famous Four

Just like a syringe, a poisonous snake has two hollow teeth called **fangs**. When it bites, the poison enters the person's body through these fangs. But here is the surprising fact: Out of many kinds of snakes in India, **only four types are poisonous**! They are the Cobra, Common Krait, Russell's Viper (Duboiya), and Saw-scaled Viper (Afai).

content.definition: The long, sharp, and hollow teeth of a poisonous snake used to inject venom.

content.text: Remembering the 4 poisonous snakes in India can be easy. Just remember '3 C's and an S': Cobra, Common Krait, (C)Russell's Viper, and Saw-scaled Viper!
A common mistake is believing that all snakes are poisonous. In reality, most snakes are not poisonous and they are actually the farmer's friends because they eat rats in the fields!

content.question: Which of the following is NOT one of the 4 poisonous snakes found in India?

text:
## 6. Reflection

Most snakes actually help humans by controlling the rat population in farms. Without snakes, rats would eat all the crops! If they are our friends, why do you think people still kill them as soon as they see them?

## 7. Connection: Venom and Cure

Did you know that the medicine for snakebite is actually made from the snake's poison? This medicine is kept in all government hospitals. It shows how nature provides both the danger and the cure!

content.text:
## 8. Mastery: The Expert Guide

Imagine you are an expert forest guide. A tourist asks you, 'What should I do if a snake bites someone?' Write a short 3-step guide for them, mentioning the hollow fangs and the government hospital medicine.
